## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.98563.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.98563.3.sa3)

Yonk and colleagues investigate the role of the thalamostriatal pathway. Specifically, they studied the interaction of the posterior thalamic nucleus (PO) and the dorsolateral striatum in the mouse. First, they characterize connectivity by recording DLS neurons in in vitro slices and optogenetically activating PO terminals. PO is observed to establish depressing synapses onto D1 and D2 spiny neurons as well as PV neurons. Second, the image PO axons are imaged by fiber photometry in mice trained to discriminate textures. Initially, no trial-locked activity is observed, but as the mice learn PO develops responses timed to the audio cue that marks the start of the trial and precedes touch. PO does appear to encode the tactile stimulus type or outcome. Optogenetic suppression of PO terminals in striatum slow task acquisition. The authors conclude that PO provides a "behaviorally relevant arousal-related signal" and that this signal "primes" striatal circuitry for sensory processing.

A great strength of this paper is its timeliness. Thalamostriatal processing has received almost no attention in the past, and the field has become very interested in the possible functions of PO. Additionally, the experiments exploit multiple cutting-edge techniques.

There seem to be some technical/analytical weaknesses. The in vitro experiments appear to have some contamination of nearby thalamic nuclei by the virus delivering the opsin, which could change the interpretation. Some of the statistical analysis of these data also appear inappropriate. The correlative analysis of Pom activity in vivo, licking, and pupil could be more convincingly done.

The bigger weakness is conceptual - why should striatal circuitry need "priming" by thalamus in order to process sensory stimuli? Why would such circuitry even be necessary? Why is a sensory signal from cortex insufficient? Why should the animal more slowly learn the task? How does this fit with existing ideas of striatal plasticity? It is unclear from the experiments that the thalamostriatal pathway exists for priming sensory processing. In fact the optogenetic suppression of the thalamostriatal pathway seems to speak against that idea.

Comments on revisions:

The authors have only tweaked the Discussion and not necessarily in ways that addressed our previous comments. They could have fairly easily analyzed the effect of distance of recording from injection site and compared subsets of data depending on contamination beyond PO (my comments 1 and 2) or effects of movements (3 and 4). Minimally, they could have given caveats in the Results and Discussion about these, and I would strongly encourage them to be explicit about the caveats. The analyses would probably be better.

The suggestion that the effects have something to do with priming (5), seems a grasp for function of the circuit.

results.result: POm provides robust and equal-amplitude synaptic input to D1-SPNs, D2-SPNs, and PV interneurons in the striatum, with PV interneurons showing significantly shorter latency to maximum PSP amplitude compared to SPNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C39-C41, and C66 collectively demonstrate that POm provides strong synaptic connections to all three striatal cell types examined. The electrophysiological data show statistically similar PSP amplitudes across cell types (C40, p=0.4835) but significantly shorter latency in PV cells (C41, p<0.0001). The experimental design includes appropriate controls (sequential patching, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and statistical analyses.

results.result: POm-striatal synapses exhibit short-term synaptic depression across all cell types, with PV interneurons showing milder depression during train stimulation compared to D1- and D2-SPNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by paired-pulse ratio and train stimulation experiments. While PPR showed no significant differences between cell types (C42, p=0.0688), train stimulation revealed significantly milder depression in PV interneurons compared to both SPN types (C44, p=0.0184 and p=0.0481). The data are consistent with known properties of synaptic plasticity.

results.result: Mice rapidly learned the whisker-based tactile discrimination task, achieving expert performance in an average of 7.6±0.51 sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by behavioral data showing increased Hit rate and decreased FA rate across training (Figure 2E). The expert criterion (Hit Rate ≥0.80 and FA Rate ≤0.30 for two consecutive sessions) is clearly defined and consistently applied. Sample size (n=5) is modest but adequate for behavioral studies.

results.result: POm-striatal axonal calcium activity significantly increased across learning phases (Shaping to Expert) but regressed to baseline levels during the Reward session, as measured by both maximum amplitude and auROC values.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are well-supported by fiber photometry data with appropriate statistical analyses (repeated measures ANOVA, p<0.0001 for both measures). The regression to baseline during the Reward session (C49, C51) provides important control evidence that the signal is not simply reward-related. The use of two complementary measures (amplitude and auROC) strengthens the findings.

results.result: POm-striatal calcium activity and pupil dilation are tightly correlated but decouple during the presentation time window, with pupil dilation lagging POm activity by approximately 250ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by simultaneous recording of calcium signals and pupil dynamics (Figure 3A, G, H). The temporal relationship is quantified through cross-correlation analysis. The findings are consistent with prior literature (Petty et al., 2021; La Terra et al., 2022), providing validation. However, the manuscript could benefit from more detailed statistical analysis of the correlation strength.

results.result: POm-striatal calcium activity remains consistent between Go and NoGo texture presentations, indicating that these projections do not encode texture-specific sensory information.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by two-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of behavioral time point (p<0.0001) but not texture type (p=0.5549) on calcium amplitude (C55). The consistency of calcium signals across texture types (C54) contrasts with divergent licking and pupil responses, strengthening the interpretation that POm-striatal signals are not sensory-specific (C56-C57).

results.result: POm-striatal calcium activity remains consistent across different trial outcomes (Hit, Miss, FA, CR), suggesting these projections do not encode outcome-specific information.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by analysis showing calcium activity consistency across trial outcomes (Figure 3M-P, 3Q) despite outcome-dependent differences in licking and pupil dynamics. The main effect of trial outcome was significant (p=0.0231), but post-hoc comparisons only showed differences between specific Shaping conditions, not across learning phases, supporting the interpretation of outcome-independence.

results.result: Optogenetic inhibition of POm-striatal axons during learning significantly delayed acquisition of expert performance (12.5 vs 7.4-7.6 sessions) and slowed reaction times, with decreased overall responding bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by optogenetic manipulation experiments with appropriate controls (No Stim and FP cohorts). The JAWS cohort required significantly more sessions (p=0.0041, C60), showed slower RTs (p=0.0124, C62), and decreased bias (p=0.0351, C61). The causal interpretation (C63) is reasonable given the experimental design, though the sample size (n=4 JAWS mice) is modest.

results.result: POm-striatal inputs provide a behaviorally relevant arousal-related signal that may prime striatal circuitry for efficient integration of subsequent choice-related inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C64 represent interpretations of the experimental data. While C10 is reasonably supported by the photometry and optogenetic results showing arousal-related activation and behavioral necessity, the 'priming' hypothesis (C11, C64) is speculative. The manuscript acknowledges this with 'may prime' language. Direct evidence for priming (e.g., demonstrating enhanced responses to subsequent inputs) is not provided, making this interpretation uncertain despite being plausible.

results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C24 represent well-established anatomical and functional knowledge about POm, supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These provide appropriate context for the current study. The authors correctly cite relevant work and accurately represent the state of knowledge in the field.

results.result: Background claims about striatal anatomy, cell types, and inputs are established from prior literature.

These provide necessary context for understanding the significance of POm-striatal projections and comparison with other thalamic inputs (particularly Pf). The literature review is comprehensive and accurate.

C65 is supported by citations, C66 by current data and comparison to Lee et al. 2019, and C67-C71 by recent literature on striatal GABA signaling (particularly Day et al., 2024). These claims appropriately contextualize the findings within existing knowledge.

results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 provide important context from prior literature about POm regulation and behavioral correlates. results.evaluation: Claims C81-C93 provide important comparative context (POm vs Pf) and acknowledge POm heterogeneity and complexity. These are well-supported by citations and help frame the limitations and future directions of the work. The acknowledgment of potential signal contamination from cortical axons (C93) and POm heterogeneity (C89-C92) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: POm provides robust synaptic input to D1-SPNs, D2-SPNs, and PV interneurons in the dorsal striatum, with relatively equal PSP amplitudes across cell types but shorter latency to peak in PV cells. The PSP amplitudes are similar to M1 inputs and larger than S1 inputs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the connectivity data but express concern about potential viral contamination of nearby thalamic nuclei (particularly VPM/VB), which could confound interpretation. One reviewer notes 'there are hardly any fibres in neocortical layer 1 while there seems to be quite a lot of them in layer 4, suggesting that the animal here was injected in the VB' and states 'the interpretation, due partly to the lack of control (especially relative to VPM contamination), is difficult.' Another reviewer mentions 'technical/analytical weaknesses' including 'contamination of nearby thalamic nuclei by the virus.'

results.result: All cell types exhibited synaptic depression in response to paired-pulse and train stimulation, but PV interneurons showed milder depression compared to SPNs during train stimulation, particularly between pulses 5-15.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the short-term plasticity findings. The data on synaptic depression patterns are presented as part of the comprehensive characterization of POm-striatal connectivity, and reviewers acknowledge the 'comprehensive description of the POm projections to the DLS.'

results.result: POm-striatal projections display learning-related activation during a whisker-based tactile discrimination task, with calcium amplitude and auROC values significantly increasing from Shaping through Expert stages, then regressing to baseline during Reward-only sessions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the progressive increase in POm activity with learning but raise concerns about interpretation. One reviewer notes the data 'do not allow to conclude if more neurones are recruited during the learning process or if the already activated fibres get activated more strongly' due to the fiber photometry method. Another reviewer suggests 'the correlative analysis of Pom activity in vivo, licking, and pupil could be more convincingly done' and notes concerns about 'effects of movements' that were not adequately addressed. The small sample size (n=5 mice) is also flagged as a weakness.

results.result: POm-striatal activation correlates with anticipatory pupil dilation but not reward-related pupil dilation, with pupil dilation lagging POm activity by approximately 250ms. The two signals are tightly correlated but decouple during the post-texture window.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the correlation between POm activity and anticipatory arousal. The editor summary states reviewers 'provide solid evidence that posterior medial thalamic nucleus (POm) terminals in striatum are activated during reward expectation and arousal.' One reviewer notes 'The results show convincingly that POm axons in the DLS are not activated by the outcome of the task but by the whisker activity.'

results.result: POm axonal activity remained consistent between Go and NoGo conditions and across different trial outcomes, indicating that POm-striatal projections do not encode texture-specific or outcome-specific sensory information but rather represent a behaviorally relevant arousal-related signal.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. One reviewer states 'The results show convincingly that POm axons in the DLS are not activated by the outcome of the task but by the whisker activity, and that this activity in average increases with learning.' The editor summary confirms reviewers provided 'solid evidence' for the arousal-related nature of the signal.

results.result: Optogenetic inhibition of POm-striatal axons during learning caused slower reaction times and increased the number of training sessions required to reach expert performance (12.5 vs 7.6 sessions), with decreased overall responding bias during the learning phase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise significant concerns about the interpretation of optogenetic inhibition results. One reviewer notes 'because POm fibres in the DLS are also projecting to S1, silencing the POm fibres in the DLS could have affected inputs in S1 as well and therefore, the slowdown in acquiring the task is not necessarily specific to the POm to DLS pathway.' Another reviewer questions the conceptual framework, asking 'why should the animal more slowly learn the task?' and states 'It is unclear from the experiments that the thalamostriatal pathway exists for priming sensory processing. In fact the optogenetic suppression of the thalamostriatal pathway seems to speak against that idea.' Sample sizes are also noted as 'on the small side.'

results.result: POm-striatal inputs provide a behaviorally relevant arousal-related signal that may prime striatal circuitry for efficient integration of subsequent choice-related inputs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express skepticism about the 'priming' interpretation. One reviewer states 'The bigger weakness is conceptual - why should striatal circuitry need "priming" by thalamus in order to process sensory stimuli? Why would such circuitry even be necessary? Why is a sensory signal from cortex insufficient?' In revision comments, the same reviewer notes 'The suggestion that the effects have something to do with priming (5), seems a grasp for function of the circuit.' The editor summary also notes 'The overall function of this pathway and the degree to which results are confounded by viral contamination of surrounding nuclei and movements remain open questions.'

results.result: Mice in the fiber photometry cohort rapidly learned to discriminate between two textures, taking an average of 7.6±0.51 sessions to become Experts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the basic behavioral learning data. One reviewer notes the authors 'used a carefully designed sensorimotor association task' and acknowledges the mice learned the discrimination.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate POm-striatal connectivity claims (C2-C4, C39-C41, C66). OpenEval finds the data SUPPORTED with appropriate controls and statistics. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN due to concerns about viral contamination of nearby thalamic nuclei (VPM/VB), which could confound interpretation of the connectivity patterns.

Both address short-term plasticity findings (C42-C44). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on paired-pulse ratio and train stimulation data. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging this as part of comprehensive POm-striatal characterization without raising specific concerns.

Both evaluate behavioral learning data (C45-C46). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with modest but adequate sample size. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging the carefully designed task and successful discrimination learning without challenging the basic behavioral findings.

Both address fiber photometry data showing learning-related POm activity increases (C47-C51). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with strong statistical evidence. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about whether more neurons are recruited vs. existing neurons activated more strongly, movement artifacts, and small sample size (n=5).

Both evaluate POm-pupil correlation claims (C52-C53). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on cross-correlation analysis and consistency with prior literature, though notes need for more detailed statistics. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting the correlation between POm activity and anticipatory arousal as solid evidence.

Both address texture-independence and outcome-independence of POm signals (C54-C57 for OpenEval; C54-C59 for peer review). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on two-way ANOVA showing no texture effect. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, finding convincing evidence that POm is not activated by task outcome but by whisker activity.

OpenEval evaluates outcome-independence claims (C58-C59) as SUPPORTED. Peer review R5 addresses overlapping claims (C58-C59) along with texture-independence, rating SUPPORTED and noting convincing evidence that POm activity is not outcome-dependent.

Both evaluate optogenetic inhibition results (C60-C63, plus C8-C9 in peer review). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with appropriate controls despite modest sample size. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about pathway specificity (POm fibers also project to S1), conceptual framework issues, and small sample sizes.

Both address the 'priming' hypothesis (C10-C11, C64). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting the interpretation is speculative without direct evidence for priming despite being plausible. Peer reviewers also rate UNCERTAIN, expressing skepticism about why striatal circuitry would need thalamic priming and questioning the conceptual framework.

OpenEval evaluates background literature claims about POm anatomy and function (C1, C12-C24) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims.
OpenEval evaluates background literature on striatal circuitry (C25-C38) as SUPPORTED with comprehensive citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluates mechanistic interpretation claims integrating current findings with prior literature (C65-C71) as SUPPORTED. While peer review R1 shares claim C66, it focuses on connectivity concerns rather than mechanistic integration.

OpenEval evaluates background literature on POm regulation and behavioral correlates (C72-C80) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluates comparative context and acknowledgment of POm heterogeneity (C81-C93) as SUPPORTED, noting appropriate scientific caution. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers do raise similar concerns about signal contamination and complexity.
